title: {{NAME}} and the Clockwork Kingdom Below
moral: Understanding something different from yourself begins with listening instead of explaining.

pages.content: The palace of Ferric Orvand existed in the deep rock beneath a mountain that everyone in the valley above simply called the Old One, as if it had been there so long it had earned the right to a title rather than a name. {{NAME}} had been brought here as a diplomatic envoy, a role he had not expected and had needed spelled out to him twice. Princess Thessaly of the surface kingdom had explained it in her direct, no-frills way: 'The Clockwork Kingdom has not spoken to anyone above-ground in sixty years. Their robots sealed the tunnels. We don't know why. You are good at talking to things that don't want to talk.' Below the mountain, the underground palace was a place of extraordinary beauty: vast chambers whose ceilings were set with glowing amber diodes that mimicked stars, corridors of polished basalt so smooth they reflected everything, and everywhere the sound of machinery, breathing, thinking, building. In the throne hall, something enormous raised its head to look at him. A Stegosaurus, her plates inlaid with circuits that pulsed faintly blue. She was the queen.

pages.content: The Stegosaurus queen's name was Vesper, and she communicated through a robot interpreter named LATCH, a slender machine with articulated fingers and a voice like polished wood. Vesper's own communication was a series of resonant plate-vibrations, complex and precise, that LATCH rendered into speech with the care of someone translating poetry. 'She says,' LATCH said, 'that the surface kingdom has never once asked what the Clockwork Kingdom needs. They have only ever told us what they need from us.' {{NAME}} thought about this. Then he asked LATCH to ask what the Clockwork Kingdom needed. This apparently surprised everyone in the throne hall considerably. LATCH's articulated fingers paused in mid-air. Vesper's plates vibrated in a pattern that LATCH translated as 'clarification requested.' 'What do you need?' {{NAME}} said simply. The hall went very quiet. Vesper's circuit-plates pulsed a slow, deep blue. When LATCH finally spoke, the robot's voice was quieter than before. 'She says she has been waiting sixty years for someone to ask that question.'

pages.content: What the Clockwork Kingdom needed was simpler and more fundamental than anything {{NAME}} had imagined. The amber diode-stars in the palace ceilings, thousands of them, were failing one by one, and the darkness spreading through the underground halls was not merely an inconvenience but a genuine crisis for a population that had lived in careful, crafted light for three hundred years. The robots could replace the diodes individually, but they could not reach the highest vaults without scaffolding they did not know how to construct, because scaffolding was surface knowledge and the surface had not spoken to them in sixty years. LATCH showed {{NAME}} the failing vaults: entire wings of the palace dimming, the dinosaur residents clustered in the lit areas, their circuits running low, a low distress pulse moving through the walls. Back at the surface, {{NAME}} described the problem to Princess Thessaly in specific and detailed terms. She was already moving before he had finished. 'I know seventeen ways to scaffold a vault,' she said. 'I built half the observatory roof myself.' She picked up her engineering satchel. 'Tell LATCH to clear the east wing. We'll start there.'

pages.content: Princess Thessaly was magnificent at scaffolding. She worked with the kind of focused, joyful competence that makes watching a skilled person work feel like a privilege, her hands sure and fast, calling directions to LATCH and the clockwork robot team with a clarity that translated easily across species and language. {{NAME}} carried components and passed tools and asked questions that Thessaly answered without slowing down. By the time they reached the east wing's highest vault, working from LATCH's instructions and Thessaly's knowledge together, they had developed a system that could replace a diode in under three minutes. When the first dark vault blazed back to full amber light, Vesper stood below it with all her circuit-plates blazing, a pattern LATCH described simply as 'joy.' The circuit-pulse of distress that had moved through the palace walls went silent. In its place came something else, a low, resonant hum that every robot in the palace began producing in unison, all at slightly different frequencies, a chord that filled the basalt chambers and rose through the rock above them and, if you stood in the valley and pressed your ear against the mountain, you could hear it.

pages.content: The feast that followed was an experience {{NAME}} suspected he would spend the rest of his life trying to describe. The Clockwork Kingdom's dining was not about food exactly, but about calibrated light and sound, each course a different arrangement of amber diodes and robot harmonics that produced in the guests a warm cascade of sensation. LATCH sat beside {{NAME}} and helpfully narrated each course. 'This one,' it said, as the hall shifted to a deep rose-amber, 'is their equivalent of warm bread.' {{NAME}} did, inexplicably, feel the sensation of warm bread. He also felt the sensation of being somewhere very safe and very understood. Princess Thessaly sat across from him, deep in conversation with Vesper via LATCH, already discussing the spring equinox exchange program she had apparently been designing in her head since the east wing lit up. At the end of the feast, Vesper pressed one great plate-flank gently against {{NAME}}'s back, and LATCH said: 'She says you asked the right question.' He slept in the palace that night on a bed of warm circuitry, and dreamed of light spreading from place to place, and in the morning he could hear the mountain humming.
